deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics. It is a set of reading notes, in German with some Greek, on Heinrich Ritter's 'Versuch zur Verständigung über die neueste deutsche Philosophie seit Kant' (Braunschweig 1853). Ritter was the Göttingen philosopher. The header reads 'Heinr. Ritter Versuch (Braunschw. 1853) über d[ie] d[eu]tsch[e] Phil[osophie] seit Kant'.

The notes are keyed to Ritter's page numbers (S. 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 12, 15). They summarise and criticise his theses.

(1) Pages 2-7 concern the Good as the Absolute. Fichte is said to treat the Good as more than an ideal (cf. S. 12 and 15). The notes also take up the idea of philosophy's history as progress ('wenn die Menschheit immer besser…'). They ask what it would mean if the universe were not the work of human beings, or if Spirit 'dictated' it.

(2) Page 8 concerns necessity versus unavoidability. The writer revises Ritter's 'nothwendig' to 'unvermeidlich'. Every empirical synthesis is unavoidable for the individual case or individual subject. It is not objectively necessary. 'Für uns' (for us) is only a special case of the conditions under which something is necessary.

(3) A historical analogy follows. Kant reacted against French and English eudaemonism, scepticism, atheism and materialism, as Luther reacted against Romanism. Kant fought servitude to matter (natural drives); Luther fought servitude under the papal slipper. Both stood on conscience. Hellenic elements (Eleatics, Heraclitus, Socrates, Plato) are said to suit the support of such struggles.

(4) A paragraph marked '+' concerns what remains for philosophy. It turns on the opposition between images or ideas and objective, unmediated versus mediated, subjective presuppositions.

(5) The next paragraph concerns post-Kantian idealism. Once idealism cut off the basis of Kant's development, namely affection from outside and the thing-in-itself, reality was lost and speculation became 'ideal'. The Aristotelian triad δύναμις / ἐνέργεια / ἐντελέχεια is invoked for a forming, building power ('bildende Kraft'), with a reference to Hegel ('Hgl.').

(6) The final lines contain a 'C. Heft' note on Fichte's development, Monadology, and Ritter's conception of the history of philosophy.

Marginal notes refer to 'Noten … Kritik', to Herbart's metaphysics and psychology ('Herb. Metaphysik … Psychol.'), and to 'Vergl. Fichte … Heft 6'.

The only numeral that looks mathematical, '4/5' in 'Vergl. S. 4: … 4/5', is a textual or page reference, not a computation.
errors: No mathematical derivations present, so no mathematical errors can be assessed.

results.what: Reading notes and critique of H. Ritter's 1853 book on German philosophy since Kant. Topics: necessity vs. unavoidability of empirical synthesis; Kant–Luther analogy; idealism's abandonment of the thing-in-itself; Aristotelian dynamis/energeia/entelecheia.
results.usually_credited_to: Heinrich Ritter (the text commented on); Kant, Fichte, Hegel, Herbart, Aristotle (the ideas discussed)

deep.surprise_reason: The page holds purely philosophical reading notes with no mathematics. Riemann's interest in philosophy, especially Herbart, is well documented, and his philosophical fragments are partly published. Notes on a Göttingen colleague's book are unremarkable.
transcription_corrections: The header is best read as 'Heinr. Ritter Versuch (Braunschw. 1853) über d. dtsch. Phil. seit Kant'. This matches Ritter's 'Versuch zur Verständigung über die neueste deutsche Philosophie seit Kant', Braunschweig 1853. 'Gesch. d. Phil.' in the header is doubtful.

In section 3.) / 8., the corrections are 'unvermeidliche' replacing 'nothwendige' and 'jedesmaligen' replacing 'bestimmten'. The transcription renders these correctly, and they carry the argument (unavoidable ≠ necessary).
In 'Kant reagirte gegen französ. engl. Eudämonism, Skepticism, Atheism, Materialism' the reading is good. 'Verwandtschaft aller Religionen' is uncertain; the image may read differently.
The '4/5' in the 'Vergl. S. 4' gloss is a textual reference, not a mathematical fraction.
The Greek terms are δύναμις, ἐνέργεια and ἐντελέχεια (Aristotelian), correctly identified.
